subject: The World Around Us
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 13 periods = 520 minutes
Total: 13 periods · 8h 40min

periods.activity_title: Into the Forest: Solar Village Story
periods.textbook_anchor: A Journey Through a Forest — reading the narrative of Reena and Amit travelling to a solar-powered village for the harvest festival (p. 57)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook illustration of a forest journey and solar-powered village

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the opening story aloud while students follow in Textbook p. 57; students listen and notice details about the forest, the village, and the two celebrations happening at once.

Whole-class discussion: What are two things being celebrated in this village at the same time? Students share what they already know about solar energy and harvest festivals — teacher accepts all responses and builds a shared picture on the board.

Students work in pairs to answer two prompts in their notebooks: (a) Why might a village celebrate becoming solar-powered? (b) What do you imagine a harvest festival looks, sounds, and smells like? Pairs share briefly with the class.

Teacher draws the pair of ideas — clean energy and harvests — together with an open question: How might the natural world and a community's celebrations be connected? Students jot one thought to close.

periods.implied_lo: Students can explain how a story's setting establishes a connection between a natural resource and a community celebration.
periods.section_context: Reena and Amit's journey to a forest-edge village, harvest festival, solar-powered village milestone.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask students whether anyone has visited a village or attended a harvest celebration — their stories ground the narrative before reading begins. Keep the closing question genuinely open; there is no single right answer at this stage.

periods.activity_title: Flame of the Forest: Local Flower Names Inquiry
periods.textbook_anchor: Welcome to the Village! — writing names of five colourful flowers found in the local area and noting regional names such as Palash/Kesuda (p. 58)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook image of the Palash tree in bloom

time_bands.activity: Teacher shows the Palash image in Textbook p. 58 and introduces the idea that many plants carry different names in different regions — Palash in Hindi, Kesuda in Gujarat. Class briefly discusses: do we know a plant by more than one name where we live?

Students work individually to recall and record five colourful flowers they have seen in their area. For each flower they write: the name they use at home, any other name they know, and a brief description of the colour and where they usually see it — following the prompt on Textbook p. 58.

Students share their lists in groups of four. The group notices which flowers appear on several lists and which are unique to one student, then picks two flowers to present to the class with both their names.
Brief class discussion: What does it tell us that the same flower has many names? Teacher notes that local knowledge of plants is valuable and is worth collecting.

periods.implied_lo: Students can record and compare local observations about the natural environment, noting regional variation in names and descriptions.
periods.section_context: Palash tree (flame of the forest), Kesuda (Gujarati regional name), five locally known colourful flowers.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Prompt students whose home language differs from the medium of instruction to share the flower name from their language — this is exactly the regional knowledge the activity values. Accept drawings alongside written names for students who find naming difficult.

periods.activity_title: Clay, Hay, and Dung: Building a Village House Model
periods.textbook_anchor: Welcome to the Village! — making a model house using natural materials such as clay, wooden sticks, hay, grass, and leaves, and decorating it with an art form (p. 60)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook images of clay-and-hay village houses with wall paintings

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the description of village houses in Textbook p. 60 — clay walls, hay roofs, cow-dung coatings, rice-flour wall paintings. Class discusses briefly: Why might villagers use these particular materials rather than bricks or cement?

Students build a small model house using the available natural materials. They first shape walls from clay, press in hay or dry grass for the roof, and use twigs as door and window frames. In the final minutes of building, each student adds a simple decorative pattern — dots, lines, or leaf prints — on one wall as a nod to traditional wall art.

A gallery walk: models are placed on desks and students move around to observe each other's work. Each student chooses one model different from their own and tells its maker one thing they noticed about the materials used.
Teacher closes by asking: Which natural material in the model do you think works best, and why? One or two students respond aloud.

periods.implied_lo: Students can construct a simple representation of a built environment using locally available natural materials and explain the function of those materials.
periods.section_context: Clay, hay, cow dung, wooden sticks, rice-flour wall paintings, traditional village house construction.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask whether any student has seen a house — or a wall, floor, or courtyard — made from clay or cow dung at home or in a relative's village; their first-hand account makes the activity tangible for the whole class. Keep the gallery walk brisk so the model-sharing stays energetic.

periods.activity_title: Colours from Nature: Preparing a Plant Dye
periods.textbook_anchor: Welcome to the Village! — preparing a natural dye from flowers, leaves, or roots such as beetroot, hibiscus, or marigold, straining the liquid, and painting a cloth with the result (p. 60)
materials: Plant materials with colour (beetroot pieces, hibiscus petals, marigold petals, or turmeric)
Strainer or piece of old cloth for straining
Light-coloured fabric scraps or a plain handkerchief per group
Hot plate or stove access (or pre-boiled dye prepared by teacher)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook illustration of natural dye materials

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the procedure from Textbook p. 60: collect plant materials with colour, boil in water, strain, apply to cloth. Students read the steps together and predict — before starting — what colour the strained liquid will be and whether it will stay on cloth.

Groups carry out the procedure: place plant material in water, observe as it boils (or use pre-boiled dye if a stove is unavailable), strain the liquid, dip or brush a cloth scrap in the dye, and spread it on newspaper to begin drying. Students record their prediction and what they observe at each step in their notebooks.

Groups compare results across the class — which plant gave the deepest colour? Students discuss: What part of the plant gave most colour — the flower, leaf, or root? Did the result match their prediction?
Teacher asks: Traditional artisans have used plant dyes for centuries — what might be the advantage of a dye made from nature compared with a factory-made dye? Students respond briefly.

periods.implied_lo: Students can carry out a multi-step investigation with plant materials, record observations at each stage, and compare results across trials.
periods.section_context: Natural dyes from flowers, leaves, barks, roots; beetroot, hibiscus, marigold; boiling, straining, dyeing cloth.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: If a stove is unavailable, prepare the boiled dye extract beforehand so students still perform the straining and dyeing steps themselves — the observation sequence must be first-hand. Ask whether anyone's family uses natural colour for festival rangoli or fabric; that knowledge links the lab step to living practice.

periods.activity_title: Keeping Grains Safe: Traditional Preservation Enquiry
periods.textbook_anchor: Welcome to the Village! — finding out traditional ways of preserving grains and vegetables and filling a table with examples (p. 62)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook images of earthen pots with neem leaves and bamboo baskets coated with cow dung

time_bands.activity: Teacher shows the textbook images on Textbook p. 62 of earthen pots lined with neem leaves and bamboo baskets coated with cow dung for grain storage. Class discusses: Why would neem leaves or cow dung help keep grains safe from insects?

Students recall and share what they know from home — how do family members store rice, lentils, spices, or vegetables? Teacher collects responses on the board, grouping them by the method used: containers, natural additives, drying, and so on.

Students fill the table in Textbook p. 62 individually, writing the grain or vegetable, the traditional method used, and the natural material that does the preserving. Those who do not know an example may use one from the class discussion on the board.
Closing discussion: These methods kept food safe without electricity or chemicals — what does that tell us about the knowledge communities carried? Students offer one sentence each.

periods.implied_lo: Students can gather and organise information about traditional resource-use practices from personal and community knowledge.
periods.section_context: Earthen pots, neem leaves, bamboo baskets, cow-dung coating, traditional grain and vegetable preservation methods.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Invite students to share what their grandparents or neighbours do — practices like storing with ash, sun-drying, or using specific pots are all valid. Ask whether any of these methods are still used at home today, and whether students think they would still work well.

periods.activity_title: Plants That Heal: Medicinal Plants and First Aid
periods.textbook_anchor: Welcome to the Village! — discussing what belongs in a first-aid box and why providing first-aid is important when someone is injured (p. 63)

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the two discussion prompts from Textbook p. 63: What should a first-aid box contain? Why is first-aid important when someone is injured? Students think individually for a moment before sharing.

Class discussion on first-aid: students list items — bandage, antiseptic, cotton — and the teacher records them. Discussion moves to: which of these items might traditionally have come from plants? Students connect to any plant knowledge from home (turmeric for wounds, aloe vera for burns, tulsi for coughs).

Students fill the table on Textbook p. 63 — plant name, plant part used, and its use — drawing on their own knowledge or on ideas raised in the class discussion. Several students share their entries aloud.

Teacher closes with the question: If someone in a village far from a pharmacy got a small cut or fever, how might knowledge of plants be as important as a first-aid kit? Students respond briefly, connecting plant knowledge to everyday safety.

periods.implied_lo: Students can describe how knowledge of plants and basic first-aid supports health and emergency preparedness in everyday situations.
periods.section_context: First-aid box contents, medicinal plants, plant parts and uses, first-aid for injuries.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask whether any student has seen a family member use a plant remedy — turmeric paste on a cut, ginger for a stomach ache, neem twigs for teeth — to make the link personal. Keep the tone caring and practical rather than alarming when discussing injuries.

periods.activity_title: Festival Lights and Solar Power: Imagining Two Days Without Electricity
periods.textbook_anchor: Sparkling Light, Happy Life — imagining life without electricity for two days and discussing the changes it would bring (p. 65)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook image of the solar-lit village during the harvest festival

time_bands.activity: Teacher shows the Textbook p. 65 image of the village lit up for the harvest festival and reads the description: traditional clothes, dhol and nagada drums, prayers to nature. Students describe what they see and the teacher links it to the solar power milestone.

Discussion of the prompt from Textbook p. 65: Imagine there is no electricity in your area for two days. What changes will you see in your life? Students brainstorm in pairs — food, light, fans, phones, water pumps — then share with the class, which builds a collective list on the board.

Teacher guides the list into two columns: things made easier by electricity, and things that worked well before electricity existed. Students copy both columns into their notebooks and add one more item to each from their own thinking.

Closing reflection: The village celebrated going solar — why might clean energy feel like something worth celebrating for a village that previously had no reliable electricity? Students offer their thoughts briefly.

periods.implied_lo: Students can identify how access to energy shapes daily life and evaluate what changes when that access is limited or newly gained.
periods.section_context: Solar-powered village, harvest festival, dhol and nagada drums, two days without electricity, traditional clothes and jewels, prayers to nature.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask if anyone has experienced a power cut that lasted more than a few hours — what did the family do? That lived experience makes the thought experiment concrete. Encourage students to think beyond urban assumptions: a village managing without grid electricity has different daily rhythms.

periods.activity_title: Traditional Dance and Song: Preparing a Performance
periods.textbook_anchor: Sparkling Light, Happy Life — finding out traditional dances and songs of the region and performing a traditional dance with classmates (p. 65)

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the activity from Textbook p. 65 and explains the goal: students will identify a traditional dance or song from their region and work together to present a short piece. Brief whole-class sharing — who knows a dance or song from home, a festival, or a family celebration?

Students form groups of four or five. Each group chooses one dance or song tradition that at least one member knows. They discuss: What is it called? When is it performed? What instruments or rhythms go with it? They practise a short sequence — steps, claps, or a verse — that the group can perform together.

Each group performs their piece (or a segment of it) for the class. After each performance, one student from the performing group shares a brief sentence about the occasion or region the dance or song belongs to.

periods.implied_lo: Students can present cultural knowledge through a creative performance and articulate the community context of a traditional art form.
periods.section_context: Traditional dances and songs of different regions, harvest festival performances, dhol and nagada drums.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Affirm diversity of dance and song traditions — a garba circle, a Bihu step, a folk song in any language, or simple rhythmic clapping from a regional custom are all equally valid. For students who do not know a tradition, invite them to observe and join an existing group.

periods.activity_title: Nature Worship: Festivals and Rituals Connected to Animals and Plants
periods.textbook_anchor: Sparkling Light, Happy Life — talking to elders and finding out rituals connected to animals and plants celebrated in the locality (p. 66)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook examples of Vat Purnima, Hari Jiroti, and the Kaziranga Elephant Festival

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the examples in Textbook p. 66 — Vat Purnima (Banyan tree), Hari Jiroti (fruit-bearing trees), and the Kaziranga Elephant Festival — and introduces the idea of Sacred Groves: forest patches communities protect for worship and wildlife. Students discuss briefly: Have you seen a tree or animal that your family or community treats as special?

Students fill the table from Textbook p. 66 individually, recording rituals or festivals connected to plants or animals that they know from home, family conversations, or local observation. They note the name of the ritual, the plant or animal involved, and the occasion or season.
Pairs share their tables and notice what is common and what is different across households and regions. Class compiles a brief shared list on the board — how many different plants and animals appear?
Teacher asks: What does it mean that communities protect certain forests or animals through worship — could this also be a way of conserving nature? Students respond with a quick thought.

periods.implied_lo: Students can record and compare cultural practices connected to the natural environment, identifying the plants, animals, and occasions they involve.
periods.section_context: Vat Purnima, Hari Jiroti, Kaziranga Elephant Festival, Sacred Groves, Jenu Kurubas apology songs to bees, local nature-connected rituals.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Prompt students to recall not just large festivals but small everyday acts — a tree in the courtyard that is watered daily, a bird that is fed every morning — as these also reflect the relationship between communities and nature. The Jenu Kurubas example of singing apology songs to bees can be raised to show how deep this respect can go.

periods.activity_title: What We Take from Nature: Listing Daily Resources
periods.textbook_anchor: Sparkling Light, Happy Life — writing about the things we use from nature in our daily life (p. 67)

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the reflection prompt from Textbook p. 67: What are the things that we use from nature in our daily life? Students think silently for a moment and then share one item each — teacher notes responses on the board without editing.

Students write their individual response in their notebooks, organising what they use from nature across categories such as food, shelter, clothing, medicine, and energy. They aim to list as many as they can from memory, then add any from the board they had not written.

Students then respond to the second reflection prompt on Textbook p. 67: What challenges arise when we overuse natural resources? Using the template (water, soil, sea products, wood), they write one consequence for each resource, drawing on what they already know from the chapter and from life.

Closing discussion: Looking at how much we use from nature every day — does that change how you feel about wasting any of it? Students share a thought aloud. Teacher affirms the connection between daily use and the responsibility to conserve.

periods.implied_lo: Students can identify the natural resources they use daily and explain the consequences of overusing those resources.
periods.section_context: Natural resources used daily (food, clothing, shelter, medicine, energy), consequences of overusing water, soil, sea products, and wood.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask students to walk through a single morning — waking up, eating, getting ready for school — and name every natural resource touched in that sequence; this grounds the list in a real routine rather than an abstract exercise. Affirm that noticing dependency is the first step toward caring for resources.

periods.activity_title: Protecting Our Environment: Planning Conservation Actions
periods.textbook_anchor: Sparkling Light, Happy Life — writing about how we can protect the natural environment around us (p. 68)

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the reflection prompt from Textbook p. 68 aloud: How can we protect the natural environment around us? Students think about spaces they know — home, school, a nearby park or street — and what challenges those spaces face.

Students write their response for at least three settings: home, school, and one other place they choose. For each, they describe one specific action they can take — reducing paper waste, avoiding plastic bags, planting a sapling, leaving water for birds — drawing on the ideas introduced in the chapter as well as their own.

Pairs read each other's plans. Each pair picks one action they both wrote about and discusses: Is this action something we could actually do? What would we need? Pairs share their chosen action with the class.

Teacher closes by noting that Sacred Groves exist because communities decided to protect a patch of nature together. Ask: What would a 'Sacred Grove' for our school or neighbourhood look like? Students offer a brief imagined answer.

periods.implied_lo: Students can plan and justify specific conservation actions for familiar environments, connecting the actions to the needs of natural resources.
periods.section_context: Sacred Groves, reducing paper waste, avoiding plastic, planting trees, feeding birds, clean-up drives, protecting the environment at home, school, parks, and locality.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Keep the tone empowering rather than guilt-inducing — students should feel that the actions they choose are within their reach. Ask whether any student's family already does one of these things regularly, and celebrate that as an existing example of conservation practice.

periods.activity_title: My Herbal Garden: Designing and Drawing
periods.textbook_anchor: Sparkling Light, Happy Life — designing a herbal garden by drawing favourite herbs in different parts of the garden and labelling them (p. 68)

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the drawing prompt from Textbook p. 68: Design a herbal garden — draw your favourite herbs in different parts and label them; also include herbs you like less. Whole-class quick brainstorm: What herbs do students know? Teacher lists them on the board — tulsi, mint, curry leaf, aloe vera, coriander, ginger, neem.

Students plan and draw their herbal garden on a full page. They divide the page into sections (beds, pots, corners) and place their chosen herbs, labelling each with its name and one use they know. They include at least one herb they like less or do not know well, and label it with a question if they are unsure of its use.

Students share their drawings in groups of three. Each student points out one herb in their garden and says why they placed it there — a favourite flavour, a remedy they know, or a plant they want to learn about. Teacher invites one or two to share with the whole class.

periods.implied_lo: Students can represent knowledge of useful plants visually, organising and labelling them according to their own understanding and preferences.
periods.section_context: Herbal garden design, favourite herbs, herb names and uses, herbs the student knows less well.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Encourage students to include herbs specific to their region or family kitchen — curry leaf in South India, fenugreek in Gujarat, mustard in Bengal — so the garden reflects real local knowledge. The herbs they 'like less' or are uncertain about are as interesting as their favourites; validate curiosity over correctness.

periods.activity_title: Growing up with Nature: A Whole-Chapter Reflection and Connection
periods.textbook_anchor: Sparkling Light, Happy Life — reflecting on how we protect the natural environment and what we use from nature (p. 68)
periods.visual_aids: Teacher-drawn mind-map framework on the board connecting forests, traditional practices, conservation, and celebrations

time_bands.activity: Teacher draws a simple mind-map on the board with 'Nature and Community' at the centre and four branches: Natural Materials and Resources, Traditional Knowledge and Crafts, Festivals and Nature Worship, and Conservation and Care. Students call out ideas from the chapter that belong on each branch, and the teacher maps them.

Discussion moves through each branch in turn. For Natural Materials: What materials from forests and plants did this chapter show being used for houses, grain storage, and dyes? For Traditional Knowledge: What practices — wall painting, neem-lined pots, natural dyes, medicinal plants — show that communities have always known how to work with nature? For Festivals and Nature Worship: What do celebrations like Vat Purnima, Hari Jiroti, and the harvest festival tell us about how communities feel about nature? For Conservation and Care: What concrete actions did the chapter connect to protecting nature — at the level of a village, a community, and an individual?

Students write three sentences in their notebooks that capture what they find most important from across the whole chapter. The three sentences must each begin differently: 'Nature gives us…', 'Communities have traditionally…', and 'I can…'. Students share with a partner before two or three share with the class.

Teacher closes with the open question: The chapter is called 'Growing up with Nature' — after everything we have explored, what do you think that title really means? Students offer their interpretations and the class ends with those voices.

periods.implied_lo: Students can draw connections across the chapter's themes — natural resources, traditional practices, cultural celebrations, and conservation — and articulate a personal meaning from the whole.
periods.section_context: Forests and natural materials, traditional craft and preservation practices, nature-worship festivals, Sacred Groves, daily resource use, conservation actions, herbal knowledge, solar energy as clean resource.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Because this synthesis draws on content from all three sections, guide the mind-map branches to surface ideas from the village arrival, the traditional knowledge activities, and the harvest festival equally — ensure no section is silent on the board. The closing question has no single answer; welcome every interpretation as a genuine reflection.

assessment_items.question_text: In the story, Reena and Amit's village was celebrating two things at the same time. Which pair correctly names BOTH celebrations?

options.label: A
options.text: A dance festival and the arrival of electricity from the city grid

options.label: B
options.text: A harvest festival and the opening of a new school

options.label: C
options.text: A harvest festival and the village becoming fully solar-powered

options.label: D
options.text: A rain festival and the village getting clean drinking water

assessment_items.annotation: Award 1 mark for A. Options B, C, and D each replace one celebration with a plausible but incorrect alternative drawn from the chapter's broader context.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can explain how a story's setting establishes a connection between a natural resource and a community celebration.

competency.competency_text: Describes the relationship between the natural environment and cultural practices in their immediate environment (nature of work, food, festivals, traditions)

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student recognised the harvest festival but substituted a generic community event for the solar-power milestone, suggesting they did not read the setting details carefully.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student confused the energy theme (solar) with a water theme, and the harvest festival with a rain festival — a compound substitution error showing partial engagement with the story.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student correctly sensed an energy theme but replaced solar power with city-grid electricity, inverting the chapter's clean-energy message, and shifted the harvest festival to a dance festival.

assessment_items.question_text: The Palash tree is called 'flame of the forest'. It is also known by the name Kesuda in Gujarat. In your area, do you know a plant or tree that is called by different names in different languages or regions? Write the plant's name and the two names you know for it.
expected_elements: Names a specific plant or tree that the student knows from their local area.
Provides at least two names for it — one in a local language or regional name and one in another language, or notes that the plant is also known by a Hindi, English, or other regional name.
The two names are clearly linked to the same plant.
assessment_items.annotation: Award full marks when all three expected elements are present. Accept any plant the student genuinely knows — regional and home-language names are valid and correct. This item invites region-specific answers: a student in Tamil Nadu may write 'Veppu / Neem', one in Gujarat 'Aamba / Mango', one in Bengal 'Neem / Margosa' — all are acceptable. Do not penalise for spelling variants of regional names.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can record and compare local observations about the natural environment, noting regional variation in names and descriptions.

competency.competency_text: Performs simple inquiry related to specific questions independently or in groups

expected_elements: Names a specific plant or tree that the student knows from their local area.
Provides at least two names for it — one in a local language or regional name and one in another language, or notes that the plant is also known by a Hindi, English, or other regional name.
The two names are clearly linked to the same plant.

assessment_items.task: Draw and label a model of a village house made from natural materials. Show at least three different materials in your drawing and write one sentence next to each material explaining what part of the house it is used for.
assessment_items.scaffold:
My village house drawing:
1. Material: __________ — Used for: __________
2. Material: __________ — Used for: __________
3. Material: __________ — Used for: __________
(Add more if you wish.)
format_of_output: A labelled drawing of a house
At least three written labels identifying different natural materials
One explanatory sentence per material describing its function in the house
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any set of natural materials consistent with the chapter — clay, hay, cow dung, wooden sticks, leaves, grass, bamboo, stone. There is no single correct house design. Award full credit when three or more materials are labelled and each has a functional explanation, even if brief.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can construct a simple representation of a built environment using locally available natural materials and explain the function of those materials.

competency.competency_text: Uses local materials to create simple objects (family tree, envelopes, origami animals) on their own for display or use in classroom processes

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The student can connect natural materials to their building functions, showing understanding that traditional construction is purposeful and knowledge-based.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold prompts the student to name each material and state its role — look for specificity: 'hay for the roof to keep rain out' is stronger than 'hay for the house'.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: drawing shows recognisable house features, three or more distinct natural materials are named, each label includes a clear functional link to the house. Weak: only one or two materials named, or explanations are circular ('clay is used because it is clay').
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who find drawing difficult may describe the house in words with a simple labelled diagram. Students from communities with different building traditions may draw a house reflecting their own background — accept stone, thatch, bamboo, or any locally authentic materials.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: A drawn-and-labelled format allows students to show spatial understanding of how materials fit together in a structure, which a list alone cannot reveal.

assessment_items.question_text:
A student followed these steps to make a natural dye: (1) collected hibiscus petals; (2) boiled them in water; (3) strained the liquid; (4) dipped a white cloth into the liquid.

Write TWO things the student would observe during this procedure — one during the boiling step and one after dipping the cloth.
expected_elements: An observation about what happens to the water or petals during boiling — for example, the water changes colour (takes on the colour of the petals), or the petals lose their colour into the water.
An observation about the cloth after dipping — for example, the cloth takes on the colour of the dye liquid, or the cloth changes from white to a pinkish or reddish colour.
assessment_items.annotation: Award full marks when both elements are present. The exact colour described may vary by plant (hibiscus gives pink to red; marigold gives yellow; beetroot gives deep red) — accept any colour observation that is consistent with the plant named in the question or a plant the student worked with. Do not penalise for imprecise scientific vocabulary as long as the observation is accurate.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can carry out a multi-step investigation with plant materials, record observations at each stage, and compare results across trials.

competency.competency_text: Gains familiarity with using the scientific method in investigations, as well as familiarity with other crosscutting concepts such as energy, matter, and systems that apply across the domains of science and engineering

expected_elements: An observation about what happens to the water or petals during boiling — for example, the water changes colour (takes on the colour of the petals), or the petals lose their colour into the water.
An observation about the cloth after dipping — for example, the cloth takes on the colour of the dye liquid, or the cloth changes from white to a pinkish or reddish colour.

assessment_items.question_text: People in villages have traditionally stored grains in earthen pots lined with neem leaves, or in bamboo baskets coated with cow dung. Why do you think they use neem leaves or cow dung for storing grains? Give ONE reason.
expected_elements: States that neem leaves or cow dung help to keep insects or pests away from the stored grain.
The reason connects the natural property of the material (neem's pest-repelling quality or cow dung's coating and insect-deterring property) to the purpose of safe grain storage.
assessment_items.annotation: Award full marks when the student identifies pest/insect repulsion as the function. Accept 'to protect the grain from insects/pests', 'neem keeps bugs away', or 'cow dung seals the basket so insects cannot get in' as equivalent correct responses. Do not require technical vocabulary.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can gather and organise information about traditional resource-use practices from personal and community knowledge.

competency.competency_text: Describes the relationship between the natural environment and cultural practices in their immediate environment (nature of work, food, festivals, traditions)

expected_elements: States that neem leaves or cow dung help to keep insects or pests away from the stored grain.
The reason connects the natural property of the material (neem's pest-repelling quality or cow dung's coating and insect-deterring property) to the purpose of safe grain storage.

assessment_items.question_text: Imagine someone in your neighbourhood gets a small cut while working in the garden. Your home is far from a clinic. Using what you know about first-aid and plants that can help with injuries, describe what you would do to help them. Give at least TWO steps.
look_for: Describes a basic first-aid step appropriate for a small cut — such as cleaning the wound with clean water or applying an antiseptic.
Mentions at least one plant or natural remedy that could help — such as turmeric paste (antiseptic), aloe vera (soothing), or neem (antimicrobial) — and explains briefly how it would be used.
The response shows understanding that first-aid is about preventing infection and easing pain while proper medical care is not immediately available.
Language is caring and practical rather than alarming.
assessment_items.annotation: Award marks for responses that combine a practical first-aid action with a plant-based remedy and show awareness of why first-aid matters. Accept any plant with a genuine antiseptic or soothing property known to the student's community — responses will vary by region. A student who mentions only standard first-aid items without any plant knowledge meets the first criterion but not the second; award partial credit accordingly.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can describe how knowledge of plants and basic first-aid supports health and emergency preparedness in everyday situations.

competency.competency_text: Discusses how to prepare for emergency situations (smoke, fire, small injuries, burns, electrical safety, unseasonal rains, fallen trees) based on discussions with family and community, or personal experiences

look_for: Describes a basic first-aid step appropriate for a small cut — such as cleaning the wound with clean water or applying an antiseptic.
Mentions at least one plant or natural remedy that could help — such as turmeric paste (antiseptic), aloe vera (soothing), or neem (antimicrobial) — and explains briefly how it would be used.
The response shows understanding that first-aid is about preventing infection and easing pain while proper medical care is not immediately available.
Language is caring and practical rather than alarming.

assessment_items.question_text: A village celebrated becoming fully solar-powered during its harvest festival. Which statement BEST explains why solar energy is useful for a village that previously had no reliable electricity?

options.label: A
options.text: Solar energy is useful because it comes from burning wood collected from the nearby forest.

options.label: B
options.text: Solar energy stores energy in large dams built near the village.

options.label: C
options.text: Solar energy uses sunlight, which is available in villages, to generate electricity without needing fuel to be brought in.

options.label: D
options.text: Solar energy works only at night when the sun is not present.

assessment_items.annotation: Award 1 mark for A. Each distractor represents a specific confusion about the nature of solar energy or conflates it with another energy source discussed in the chapter.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can identify how access to energy shapes daily life and evaluate what changes when that access is limited or newly gained.

competency.competency_text: Describes usage of natural resources in their immediate environment

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student confused solar energy with hydroelectric power (dams), suggesting they registered 'clean energy' but did not distinguish between solar panels and water-based energy systems.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student inverted the relationship between sunlight and solar energy — a factual misconception suggesting they did not engage with the solar-power concept in the chapter.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student conflated solar energy with the forest-based resources discussed elsewhere in the chapter, particularly wood, showing that the two resource types were not clearly distinguished.

assessment_items.task: Choose a traditional dance or song from your region (or one you know from your family or community). Write its name, describe when it is performed, and create a short verse, a set of steps, or a drawing that shows what the performance looks or sounds like.
assessment_items.scaffold:
Name of the dance or song: __________
When it is performed: __________
What it looks or sounds like (write a verse, describe steps, or draw): __________
format_of_output: Written name of the dance or song
A sentence or two about when or why it is performed
A creative representation — verse, description of steps, or a drawing showing the performance
assessment_items.annotation: There is no single correct answer. Accept any traditional dance or song that the student genuinely knows — garba, Bihu, Lavani, Kolattam, Ghoomar, a folk lullaby, a harvest song, or any other regional or family tradition. The creative representation may be minimal (a few steps described, a simple verse, or a sketch) but must exist. This item invites region-specific answers: a wide range of traditions across India are equally valid.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can present cultural knowledge through a creative performance and articulate the community context of a traditional art form.

competency.competency_text: Describes relationships (including between humans and animals/nature) and traditions (art forms, celebrations, festivals) in the family and community

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The student can draw on community and family knowledge to identify and represent a cultural art form, connecting it to the occasion or season that calls for it.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: Look for a named tradition (not just 'a dance'), a context that shows the student knows when it is performed (festival, harvest, wedding, seasonal celebration), and any creative attempt — even simple — to represent what it looks or sounds like.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: a specific named tradition, a clear occasion linked to nature or community life, and a creative representation with some detail. Weak: a vague description ('a dance at festivals') with no name and no creative element.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who do not know a regional dance may describe a family tradition, a school celebration song, or a song they have heard at a community gathering. Students who find writing difficult may draw the performance scene and label it.
OPEN_TASK.format_type: Written description with a creative element (verse, steps, or drawing)
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: This format allows students to demonstrate cultural knowledge through expression rather than recall alone, matching the creative mode of the period's activity.

assessment_items.question_text: The chapter describes festivals such as Vat Purnima (where people worship the Banyan tree) and Sacred Groves (forest patches that communities protect for worship). How do these traditions help protect nature? Give ONE way.
expected_elements: States that worshipping or protecting trees and forests through cultural or religious traditions means those trees or forests are not cut down or harmed.
The answer connects the cultural practice (worship, festival, community protection) to an outcome that benefits nature (trees preserved, animals protected, forest maintained).
assessment_items.annotation: Award full marks when the student connects the cultural practice to a conservation outcome. Accept 'if people worship a tree they will not cut it', 'Sacred Groves stay protected because the community treats them as holy', or 'animals living in a Sacred Grove are safe because no one hunts there' as equivalent correct responses.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can record and compare cultural practices connected to the natural environment, identifying the plants, animals, and occasions they involve.

competency.competency_text: Demonstrates how natural resources can be shared, maintained, and conserved (trees, use of rainwater, benefits of millets)

expected_elements: States that worshipping or protecting trees and forests through cultural or religious traditions means those trees or forests are not cut down or harmed.
The answer connects the cultural practice (worship, festival, community protection) to an outcome that benefits nature (trees preserved, animals protected, forest maintained).

assessment_items.question_text: Which of the following groups lists ONLY things that come directly from nature and are used in daily life?

options.label: A
options.text: Plastic bags, cotton, water, neem leaves

options.label: B
options.text: Wood, cotton, tap water purified by chemicals, neem leaves

options.label: D
options.text: Wood, glass bottles, water, neem leaves

assessment_items.annotation: Award 1 mark for A. Each distractor includes one human-made or processed item slipped into an otherwise natural list, testing whether students can distinguish natural from manufactured resources.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can identify the natural resources they use daily and explain the consequences of overusing those resources.

competency.competency_text: Describes usage of natural resources in their immediate environment

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student did not identify plastic as a human-made material, suggesting they have not yet distinguished manufactured products from natural resources.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student did not identify glass (a manufactured product, even if made from sand) as processed rather than directly from nature — a common and understandable confusion.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student did not recognise that chemically purified water is processed, conflating the natural resource (water) with the treated form delivered through a tap.

assessment_items.question_text: The chapter describes actions people can take to protect nature: reducing paper waste, avoiding plastic, planting trees, leaving food and water for birds, and organising clean-up drives. Choose TWO of these actions and explain, for each one, HOW it helps nature and WHERE you could do it — at home, school, or somewhere else you know.
look_for: Names two specific conservation actions from the chapter (or similar actions the student knows).

For each action, gives a clear explanation of how it benefits nature — not just 'it helps the environment' but a specific mechanism (e.g., 'planting trees gives shade and provides shelter for birds', 'avoiding plastic means animals don't swallow it by mistake').
For each action, names a specific location and links that location to the action in a way that makes sense (e.g., 'at school we could have a paper-recycling bin for used worksheets').
The overall response shows the student is thinking about conservation as something they can personally practise, not just a general concept.
assessment_items.annotation: Full marks require both actions to be explained with a mechanism and a location. Partial credit for one complete action or for two actions where location or mechanism is missing for one. Accept any conservation action grounded in the chapter even if phrased differently.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can plan and justify specific conservation actions for familiar environments, connecting the actions to the needs of natural resources.

competency.competency_text: Demonstrates how natural resources can be shared, maintained, and conserved (trees, use of rainwater, benefits of millets)

For each action, gives a clear explanation of how it benefits nature — not just 'it helps the environment' but a specific mechanism (e.g., 'planting trees gives shade and provides shelter for birds', 'avoiding plastic means animals don't swallow it by mistake').
For each action, names a specific location and links that location to the action in a way that makes sense (e.g., 'at school we could have a paper-recycling bin for used worksheets').

assessment_items.task: Design your own herbal garden on a full page. Draw at least four herbs in different parts of the garden. Label each herb with its name and write ONE use next to it. Include at least one herb you are less sure about — write a question about it instead of a use.
assessment_items.scaffold:
My herbal garden:
[Draw the garden layout — beds, pots, or sections]
For each herb write:
Name: __________
Use (or question): __________
format_of_output: A drawn garden layout with sections or beds
At least four herbs labelled with names
One use written next to each herb (or a genuine question for the uncertain herb)
assessment_items.annotation: There is no single correct garden design or required set of herbs. Accept any herbs the student genuinely knows — tulsi, mint, aloe vera, curry leaf, coriander, ginger, neem, fenugreek, or any herb from the student's regional or family knowledge. The 'uncertain herb with a question' element is intentional — it values curiosity alongside knowledge. Regional variation in herb knowledge is expected and correct.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can represent knowledge of useful plants visually, organising and labelling them according to their own understanding and preferences.

competency.competency_text: Uses local materials to create simple objects (family tree, envelopes, origami animals) on their own for display or use in classroom processes

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The student can organise and visually represent plant knowledge, showing that they connect named plants to their uses and can acknowledge the limits of their own knowledge.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: Look for a genuine attempt to arrange herbs spatially (not just a list), at least four labelled herbs with uses, and a real question for the uncertain herb — 'I don't know what this is for' is honest and valid.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: a thoughtful layout with distinct sections, four or more herbs, specific uses (not just 'it is healthy'), and a genuine inquiry question for the uncertain herb. Weak: a list of herb names without spatial arrangement or uses.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students from different regions will know different herbs; this is a strength of the item. A student who knows only two herbs by name may draw those two with detail and attempt two unfamiliar ones with questions — this meets the spirit of the task. Students who find drawing difficult may use a simple grid or map instead of a pictorial garden.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: A garden layout requires the student to think spatially and representationally about plants — skills that go beyond listing names and connect to the chapter's theme of living with and organising nature.

assessment_items.question_text:
This chapter is called 'Growing up with Nature'. It has shown how forests and plants provide materials for houses, dyes, food storage, and medicine; how communities have festivals and traditions that celebrate and protect nature; and how individuals can take actions to conserve natural resources.

In your own words, explain what you think 'growing up with nature' means. Use at least TWO ideas from the chapter to support your answer.
look_for: Offers a personal interpretation of the phrase 'growing up with nature' — not a dictionary definition but a meaningful statement about the relationship between people and the natural world.

Supports the interpretation with at least two specific ideas, examples, or practices from the chapter — such as using natural materials for building, traditional grain storage, nature-worship festivals, Sacred Groves, medicinal plants, solar energy, or conservation actions.
The response draws a connection between the two ideas chosen, showing the student sees a pattern or relationship across the chapter's themes rather than listing isolated facts.
The overall response shows that the student has engaged with the chapter's whole argument — that human life and culture are deeply intertwined with nature — and can express that in their own voice.
assessment_items.annotation: This is a synthesis item — it tests the student's ability to draw meaning across the whole chapter, not recall a single fact. Award full marks for responses that offer a genuine personal interpretation backed by two relevant chapter ideas, even if the language is simple. Do not require academic phrasing. Partial credit for responses that offer a meaningful interpretation without chapter support, or chapter details without a personal interpretation.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can draw connections across the chapter's themes — natural resources, traditional practices, cultural celebrations, and conservation — and articulate a personal meaning from the whole.
